claims_disputed.claim: Visible/public tests vastly overstate correctness relative to hidden validators.
claims_disputed.reason: The cited gap pits PublicScore, a mean over public test cases, against Pass@1, which requires every private test to pass (§5 Evaluation), so the gap mixes two different metrics. The like-for-like gap, PublicScore vs PrivateScore in Table 2, is about 21-45 pp (e.g. Claude-Opus-5 96.64% vs 75.11%). That gap is large, but it is partly built in: public materials are a reproduction script plus minimal diagnostics (Fig. 3 shows 1 public check vs 10 private cases), and hidden validators are deliberately built to defeat overfitting (§4 step 4, §4.1). Each configuration is also a single attempt.

pattern_stance_changes.reason: Every configuration has the same public tests and can run them (§3.1, Fig. 3). There is no arm without an execution loop or with a different verifier. The public/private gap describes how weak this benchmark's public tests are, not a measured effect of the verifier loop.

The §4.2/§6.2 ablation adds or removes static scientific guidance in the task materials. Nothing is disclosed progressively or loaded on demand, so progressive disclosure is not tested. The opposite-sign Pass@1 changes (8 vs 12 and 9 vs 3 discordant tasks, Fig. 7) are also not significant, as the authors state.

missed_issues: The applicability text says 'harness choice shifts outcomes', which contradicts the review's own harness_model_confound bias. Each model runs in exactly one harness (§5), so the paper cannot tell mixed-host teams anything about Codex vs Claude Code vs Kimi Code parity.

The ablation runs GPT-5.6-sol at xhigh and DeepSeek-V4-flash at high (§6.2), while Table 2 uses max. The 'with info' arm is therefore not the main condition, and ablation numbers cannot be compared with Table 2.
'Weaker models may benefit more from external scientific guidance' (§6.2) is extrapolated from two models with non-significant changes.
The evaluator metadata includes a 'contamination tier' field (§3.1), but no contamination analysis or tier-stratified result is reported, although many Issue-driven tasks have public upstream fixes.

No wall-clock, step or cost limits are reported for the agent runs, and all frontier configurations run at max effort. Token use varies widely (Fig. 5), so the Pass@1 ranking is not at matched budget.
note: I agree with the verdict and most scores; the benchmark is careful and its Table 2 and Table 3 counts check out exactly as k/n. The review has no supports stances. Its two mixed stances are for patterns no arm varies or that don't match the ablation, so they are neutral. The public-vs-hidden headline uses mismatched metrics and is partly built into the benchmark, so it is moderate rather than strong.
